lead: Multichannel EEG records many scalp voltages at once, so a clinician can see where brain activity rises, falls or synchronises. Epilepsy shows up as spikes and seizures; evoked potentials are tiny stimulus-locked responses pulled out by averaging. MEG measures the magnetic field of the same currents with SQUID sensors. These tools map brain function non-invasively in hospitals and research labs, and they share one problem: a microvolt or femtotesla signal buried in noise.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6 for EEG bandwidth and gain, Chapter 4 for differential amplifiers, and Chapter 2 for electrode impedance.

blocks.text: The 10–20 system places scalp electrodes at fixed fractions of the head. Common sites are Fp1, Fp2, C3, C4, O1, O2 and midline Fz, Cz, Pz. Odd numbers sit on the left, even numbers on the right, and z means midline. Denser caps use 64, 128 or 256 electrodes for finer spatial maps.

Each electrode feeds one channel of a multichannel amplifier. Gain is typically 10⁴ to 10⁵ and CMRR above 80 dB, because the EEG is only tens of microvolts riding on a larger common-mode voltage. Routine bandwidth is about 0.5–70 Hz.

A montage is the chosen pairing of electrodes. A referential montage compares each active electrode with one reference, such as linked ears or Cz. A bipolar montage subtracts neighbouring electrodes, for example Fp1–F3 then F3–C3. Referential shows the field at one site; bipolar rejects shared noise but can cancel a broad field. The display stacks channels, with voltage up and time across.

A seizure is a sudden, synchronous discharge of cortical neurons. On EEG it appears as spikes, sharp waves or spike-and-wave complexes. A spike lasts about 20–70 ms and a sharp wave 70–200 ms; both stand out from background, and a slow wave often follows. Absence seizures give a regular 3 Hz spike-and-wave pattern. Focal seizures give spikes in one or a few channels.

Interictal spikes occur between seizures and help locate the focus. Ictal EEG is recorded during the event, often with video. The reader compares channels and montages to separate a true cortical spike from an eye blink or electrode artefact. Spike amplitude is tens to hundreds of microvolts, larger than normal background. At a paper speed of 30 mm/s, one page shows about 10 s.

An evoked potential (EP) is a small, time-locked brain response to a stimulus. Visual EP (VEP): flash or reversing checkerboard on a screen, recorded over the occiput, with a positive peak near 100 ms called P100. Brainstem auditory EP (BAEP): click through earphones, waves I–V in the first 10 ms. Somatosensory EP (SSEP): electrical pulse to a nerve, such as the median nerve, with N20 near 20 ms. Latency is the time from stimulus to a peak, in ms. Amplitude is peak-to-peak, in µV.

The EP is buried in ongoing EEG. Averaging many stimulus-locked trials keeps the EP because it has fixed phase, and averages random noise toward zero. Artefact rejection removes trials with blinks or movement before averaging. A 50 Hz notch filter removes mains interference.

items: Give stimuli at a fixed rate.
Record EEG and reject bad trials.
Measure latency and amplitude from the averaged wave.

blocks.where: SNR<sub>1</sub> is the signal-to-noise ratio in one trial (dimensionless); N is the number of averaged trials (no unit); SNR<sub>N</sub> is the ratio after averaging.

blocks.text: Magnetoencephalography (MEG) measures the magnetic field produced by the same cortical currents that make the EEG. The field is tiny, on the order of 10–1000 fT (femtotesla; 1 fT = 10⁻¹⁵ T). A SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device) converts this flux into a voltage. It works at cryogenic temperature, so the sensors sit in a helmet cooled by liquid helium.

MEG is not distorted by the skull and scalp, so it localises sources well; temporal resolution matches EEG. Arrays have 100–300 sensors. It is used in presurgical mapping and research. EEG and MEG are often recorded together and mapped onto an MRI.

Before every recording, check each electrode impedance (below about 5 kΩ, and the electrodes similar to each other) and apply the calibration signal. A 50 µV calibration pulse should give the same deflection on every channel, about 7 mm at the usual sensitivity of 7 µV/mm, with the same decay set by the high-pass filter. Then record a short biological check: eyes open, eyes closed (alpha should appear over the occiput), blink and clench.

blocks.text: Maintenance: wash cup electrodes after each patient, re-chloride silver electrodes when the coating wears, store caps dry, and replace any lead with a cracked insulation.

figure.caption: The same 1 µV response is locked to the stimulus in every trial while the 2 µV background is not, so the average keeps the response and the noise shrinks by √N. Sixteen trials give SNR 2; the worked example's 400 trials give SNR 10 and a clear P100.

spec.aria: Three traces of a visual evoked potential after one, 16 and 400 averaged trials, the first buried in noise and the last showing a clear positive peak at 100 milliseconds, with signal-to-noise ratios of 0.5, 2 and 10.

examples.question: A visual evoked potential has amplitude 1 µV. The background EEG noise in the same band is 2 µV. Averaging improves the signal-to-noise ratio by √N. How many trials give SNR = 10? Find the single-trial SNR and the required √N first.
examples.answer: 400 trials are needed; the single-trial SNR is 0.5 and the required √N is 20.
examples.check:
snr0 = 1/2
sqrtN = 10/snr0
N = sqrtN**2
print(snr0)
print(int(sqrtN))
print(int(N))

traps: Averaging reduces random noise, not artefacts locked to the stimulus. A time-locked artefact keeps its full size in the average while the noise shrinks, so it stands out more.
Referential and bipolar montages answer different questions; a broad field may vanish in bipolar because both electrodes see it.
EP latency is in milliseconds and amplitude in microvolts. Do not swap the two.
Odd electrode numbers are on the left, even on the right; C3 is left and C4 is right.
MEG measures magnetic field in femtotesla, not scalp voltage in microvolts. The units are not interchangeable.

quiz.q: In the 10–20 system, what do odd numbers, even numbers and z mean?
quiz.a: Odd numbers are left hemisphere, even numbers are right hemisphere, and z is midline.

quiz.q: Why does a bipolar montage reject more shared noise than a referential montage?
quiz.a: It subtracts two nearby electrodes. A common signal appears at both and cancels, while the local gradient remains.

quiz.q: Single-trial SNR is 0.2. After averaging 100 trials, what is the SNR?
A 50 Hz mains hum is present in every trial at the same phase. Will averaging 400 trials remove it? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Averaging reduces random noise by √N. A fixed-phase artefact adds rather than cancels, so use a notch filter or better shielding.
VEP = visual evoked potential; BAEP = brainstem auditory evoked potential; SSEP = somatosensory evoked potential.

quiz.q: Why must eye-blink trials be rejected before VEP averaging?
quiz.a: A blink is a large fixed artefact. It can mimic or swamp the small VEP, and averaging does not remove it.

quiz.q: State one advantage of MEG over EEG.
quiz.a: Magnetic fields pass through the skull and scalp without distortion, so MEG gives better source localisation.

beyond: Not for the exam. High-density EEG and MEG are moving toward wearable helmets and optically pumped magnetometers that need no liquid helium. Source-imaging software fuses EEG or MEG with MRI for presurgical planning. Brain–computer interfaces use the same multichannel recordings. Search for event-related potential, SQUID magnetometer and EEG source localisation if you want the research path.
